text.text: Everything the agency runs on, in one place: clients and their retainers, campaigns, the deliverables inside them, time logged and the monthly reports owed. Start with the Dashboard each Monday, then work the Overdue and Mine views. Check Hours used on every client before agreeing extra work.
Clients
The brands the agency runs programs for, with their retainer terms.
Campaigns
Each program the agency runs for a client.
Deliverables
The pieces of work inside a campaign, from ad sets to landing pages.
Time entries
Hours logged against clients and campaigns, the source of every retainer figure.
Monthly reports
The report owed to each client every month.

This workspace runs an agency's client side: what each client pays and what that buys, how many hours have been used this month, which campaigns are live and how they perform, what is waiting on the client to approve, and which monthly reports are owed. Time tracking, ad platforms and invoicing stay in their own tools; the numbers that matter land here.
The lists

cells.text: Retainer, contract, notice, scope, hours used, renewal date
Goal, budget, spend, results, cost per result, deliverables waiting on the client
Kind, due date, client approval, revision rounds
One client report for a period

text.text: The numbers to watch
Hours used (%)
compares this month's time with the hours in the retainer. Near limit at 80 percent, Over at 100.
Reports owed
counts reports not started, drafting or in client review.
Ad spend managed
adds spend on every campaign past Planned.
Waiting on client approval
counts deliverables waiting or sent back with changes.
Your first week
Enter each client with the retainer, the contract length and notice period, and the scope in their words from the signed agreement.
Enter live campaigns with the goal you agreed, the budget and spend so far.
Add the deliverables due in the next two weeks and mark which need the client's approval.
Ask the team to log time daily against client and campaign.
The monthly rhythm

cells.text: Reports sent with a short call offered
Hours check: any client near the limit gets a scope talk
Renewal plan with results and next quarter's ideas

text.text: Example
Marigold Pet Supply renews in five days on a six-month contract. The account manager sends the renewal note with the bundle results and two ideas for the next quarter, and books a call the same week.
The agency at a glance. Charts read from the live tables, so they move as the team logs time and updates statuses.
Deliverables overdue
Reports waiting on us
Renewing in the next 30 days
How to read the numbers

cells.text: Hours logged this month divided by the hours included in the retainer
At 80 percent warn the client; at 100 percent agree extra hours or scope in writing
Renewal date minus today; negative means the renewal date has passed
Book the review call at 45 days; chase any negative number today
Spend to date divided by the ad budget
Over 100 means overspend; under 60 near the end means underspend
Deliverables done divided by deliverables in the campaign
Below plan at the halfway date means re-plan with the client

text.text: The monthly report is where a client decides whether the retainer is worth it. A good one is short, honest and leads with what changed for the business, not with charts.
The schedule
On the first working day, every active client gets a report row with a due date no later than the fifth.
The author pulls numbers from the ad platforms, analytics and email tool.
The account lead reviews before anything goes to the client.
Send, then press the status to
Sent
and record the date.
The shape of every report

cells.text: One sentence: the most important outcome against the goal
Each campaign's agreed goal and what happened
Budget, spend and cost per result for each paid campaign
Deliverables finished this month, in plain words
One or two honest observations, good or bad
Three planned actions, each tied to a goal

text.text: Write the
Headline result
on the report row too, so the whole team sees it without opening the file.
Writing tips
Lead with the business result: orders, booked calls, members, donations. Clicks come later.
Compare with last month and the same month last year where you can.
Explain any bad number before the client asks about it.
Keep it to what the client can read in five minutes.
Review checklist
Every number matches its source
Spend matches the platform invoices
Every campaign has its goal stated
Next month's actions are realistic for the hours left in the retainer
The call
Offer a 20-minute call with each report. Clients who talk through results renew more often than those who only receive a file.
Example

Brightwater's report is in client review and one day past due. The emergency search campaign booked more calls at a lower cost per call, so the account lead calls the owner to walk through it rather than waiting for an email reply.
The first 30 days set the tone for the whole relationship. A client who sees early structure and quick wins stays; a client who waits three weeks for access requests starts looking around.
Before the kickoff
Signed agreement with retainer, contract length, notice period and scope
First invoice paid
Client added with
Scope in the retainer
written from the agreement
Account manager and campaign leads named
Access (ask for everything in one list)
Ad accounts with admin access for your agency's business manager
Analytics and tag manager
Website or content system for landing pages and tracking
Email platform and customer lists
Brand guide, logos, photo library and past campaign results
The kickoff meeting
Agree the goal for each channel as a number the business cares about: orders, calls, members or leads. Write it into
Goal agreed with client
on each campaign.
Agree who approves work on their side, and how fast. Two working days is a fair default.
Walk through the monthly rhythm: reports by the fifth, a mid-month check, a strategy call each quarter.
Agree what is not in scope, kindly and clearly.
The first 30 days

cells.text: Access, tracking checked end to end, audit of current accounts
Quick fixes from the audit; first campaign plan shared
First new creative and landing pages to the client for approval
Campaigns live; first short update sent

text.text: Hand-over from sales
Ask whoever sold the account for the promises made in the pitch. Write any that are not in the agreement on the client, and agree with the client which ones still stand.
Tracking first
Nothing launches until conversions are tracked and tested. A test order or a test form fill, seen arriving in analytics, is the proof.
Example

Fernhill Dental is onboarding. The SEO crawl is in progress and three service area landing pages are waiting on the client's approval, so the account manager books a 15-minute call to approve them together instead of waiting for email.
A retainer buys a fixed amount of work each month. Agencies lose money quietly when the work grows and the fee does not. These rules keep both sides honest.
What the retainer covers
The scope is written on each client in
Scope in the retainer
, copied from the agreement. If a request is not in that text, it is new work.
Hours
Everyone logs time daily against the client and campaign.
Hours used this month
adds up this month's entries.
Hours used (%)
compares them with
Hours included per month

cells.text: Account lead told; non-urgent requests moved to next month
Talk to the client before more work is done

text.text: When a client asks for something new
Thank them and say you will come back with a plan.
Check the scope text. If it is in scope, schedule it.
If not, offer three choices: swap it for something planned this month, add it as a one-off project with a price, or raise the retainer.
Write down what they chose, on the client.
Revision rounds
Two rounds of changes per deliverable are normal.
Revision rounds
on each deliverable makes the third round visible. A third round usually means the brief was unclear; fix the brief, not just the work.
Renewals and notice
Renews on
and
Days to renewal
show what is coming. Start renewal talks two months ahead.
Notice period
is the days either side must give to end the agreement.
A client at Over for three months in a row needs a bigger retainer or a smaller scope at renewal.
Example
Lumen Ledger asked for a webinar landing page. It is not in their scope, so the account lead offers to swap it for one content hub article this month or quote it as a small project.
Ad spend is separate
Ad budgets are paid to the platforms, not to you. Keep the retainer and the media budget on separate lines in every conversation.
A short, fixed weekly rhythm keeps a busy agency calm: everyone knows what is due, what is waiting on clients, and where hours are running out.
Monday stand-up (20 minutes)
Deliverables due this week, by owner. Anything at risk is said out loud.
Deliverables
Waiting on client
for more than two working days. The account manager chases each one that day.
Clients near or over their hours.
Campaigns whose spend is ahead of or behind plan.
Midweek performance check
Every live paid campaign checked for spend pacing and cost per result
Any campaign more than 20 percent off its goal gets a written change: new creative, new audience or a budget shift
Changes noted on the campaign so the monthly report can explain them
Friday wrap-up
Time entries complete for the week; missing days chased.
Deliverables finished this week marked done.
One short note to each active client: what shipped, what is next, what we need from them.
Roles

cells.text: Strategy, setup and optimization of each campaign
Creative, copy, landing pages, email and tracking
Pricing, hiring, the clients at risk

text.text: Workload
If one person owns more than a fair share of deliverables due this week, move work before Monday ends. Burned-out specialists lose clients faster than any campaign.
Example

The emergency call-extension copy for Brightwater is three days overdue with changes requested twice. At the stand-up, the team agrees the account manager will get one clear brief from the owner and the copywriter will finish it the same afternoon.
Client approvals
Approvals are where weeks disappear. Send work for approval with a clear question and a date: "Approve these three ads by Wednesday so they go live Friday." Mark the deliverable
Waiting on client
the moment it goes out.
Keep the meeting short
Discuss only what is late, waiting or off track. Everything on time stays out of the meeting.
